title: Jehu Anointed: The Fall of Joram and Jezebel
summary: Elisha sends a young prophet to Ramoth-gilead to anoint the army commander Jehu king over Israel and commission him to destroy the house of Ahab. The officers proclaim Jehu king, and he drives furiously to Jezreel, where he kills King Joram of Israel on the field of Naboth and mortally wounds King Ahaziah of Judah. Jezebel meets him from her window with a taunt; her own servants throw her down, and the dogs leave almost nothing of her, as Elijah had said.
story: The long story of Ahab's house, begun in 1 Kings 16, reaches its end. Elijah was told at Horeb to anoint Jehu king of Israel (1 Kings 19:16), and after Naboth's murder he pronounced that dogs would eat Jezebel at Jezreel and that every male of Ahab's line would be cut off (1 Kings 21:19-24). God delayed that judgment when Ahab humbled himself (21:29). Now, in the days of Ahab's son, it falls. The chapter also shows the fruit of Judah's alliance with Ahab: Ahaziah of Judah, Ahab's grandson through his mother Athaliah, happens to be visiting his wounded uncle and dies with him. Chapter 10 will complete Jehu's purge, and chapter 11 will show its consequences in Jerusalem.
historical:
Jehu's coup took place in 841 BC, one of the firmest dates in the period. That same year Shalmaneser III of Assyria campaigned in the west and received tribute from Jehu. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser, discovered at Nimrud in 1846 and now in the British Museum, shows a figure bowing before the Assyrian king with a caption naming Jehu, son of Omri; the Assyrians called Israel the house of Omri even after Omri's dynasty had been overthrown. It is often described as the only known ancient depiction of an Israelite king or his envoy.

Joram had been wounded defending Ramoth-gilead against Hazael (8:28-29) and was recovering at Jezreel, a royal residence in the fertile Jezreel Valley. Ramoth-gilead, where Jehu was with the army, lay east of the Jordan, so the ride to Jezreel covered a considerable distance. Ibleam and Megiddo lay south and west of Jezreel along the valley's edge. Second Chronicles 22:7-9 gives a somewhat different account of Ahaziah's death, in which he is found hiding in Samaria and brought to Jehu; interpreters have proposed ways to harmonize the two, and some see them as independent traditions. The Aramaic Tel Dan Stele, discussed under the hard question, offers another angle on the same events.
cultural:
Anointing with oil set a person apart for an office, particularly kingship (1 Samuel 10:1; 16:13). A prophet's anointing of Jehu in secret, in an inner room, made him king in God's sight before any public acclaim. The officers' response, spreading their garments on the steps and blowing the ram's horn (verse 13), was a spontaneous coronation: the horn announced a new king, and garments laid down formed a makeshift royal carpet. The officers call the young prophet a madman (verse 11), which reflects how prophets' ecstatic behavior sometimes looked to outsiders.

Jezebel's painting of her eyes with dark cosmetic and arranging her hair (verse 30) has been read in two ways: as an attempt to seduce or manipulate Jehu, or, more likely in context, as a queen dressing in royal dignity to face death. Her greeting, calling Jehu Zimri, refers to the army commander who murdered King Elah and reigned seven days before dying in flames (1 Kings 16:9-20); it is a curse and a prophecy that Jehu will not last. To lie unburied and be eaten by dogs was among the worst fates imaginable in the ancient world, a sign of total rejection. Jehu's instruction to bury her because she was a king's daughter (verse 34) came too late.
literary: This is one of the most vivid chapters in the Old Testament, told at speed. The word peace (shalom) is its refrain. Joram's messengers ask it, Joram asks it, and Jezebel asks it, and Jehu's answer is that there can be no peace while Jezebel's idolatry and witchcraft continue (verse 22). The watchman's reports build suspense as horseman after horseman fails to return, until the driving itself identifies the rider: “he is driving like a madman” (verse 20). Place names are loaded: Joram meets Jehu on the property of Naboth the Jezreelite, and his body is thrown onto Naboth's field. The chapter is framed by prophecy. It begins with the young prophet's oracle that dogs will eat Jezebel at Jezreel (verse 10) and ends with Jehu quoting Elijah's word as fulfilled (verses 36-37). Throughout, Jehu is shown as energetic, ruthless, and quick with Scripture, a portrait that is not simply admiring.

outline.t: A young prophet anoints Jehu at Ramoth-gilead
Jehu kills Joram on Naboth's land
Ahaziah of Judah is shot and dies at Megiddo
Jezebel's death and the word of Elijah fulfilled

doctrines.note: The house of Ahab falls on the very ground Ahab stole from Naboth. God's judgment was delayed for years, but it came in the place and manner his prophet had announced, as a response to innocent blood.

Jehu twice cites the word of the LORD as fulfilled (verses 25-26, 36-37). The chapter is written to show that the prophetic word, spoken long before, governs events even when the actors are violent and self-interested.
Jehu names Jezebel's idolatry and sorcery as the reason there can be no peace (verse 22). The worship of Baal was not merely private belief; it came with the corruption of justice that killed Naboth.

words.note: Mashach, to anoint, the verb behind the word mashiach, anointed one, from which Messiah comes. The young prophet anoints Jehu, making him the LORD's chosen king for a specific task of judgment. The word shows that anointing marks God's choice and commission, not necessarily the character of the one anointed.

Shalom, peace, welfare, wholeness. The question “Have you come in peace?” is repeated four times (verses 17-22 and 31). Jehu's answer turns the word from a greeting into a verdict: shalom is impossible where the covenant is broken by idolatry and violence.

Cheleq, portion or plot of ground. The word recurs for the plot at Jezreel where Jezebel will be devoured and the plot of Naboth onto which Joram is thrown (verses 10, 21, 25, 36-37). Naboth had refused to sell his family's inheritance (1 Kings 21:3); the same ground becomes the site of the judgment on those who took it.

christ: Jehu is an anointed one, a messiah in the plain Old Testament sense, sent to execute judgment on a murderous dynasty, and the contrast with Jesus the Messiah is instructive. Jehu comes driving furiously with bow and arrows and leaves a trail of blood; Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, weeps over the city, and sheds his own blood rather than his enemies'. Both are concerned with justice for the innocent, since Naboth's blood cries out in this chapter as Abel's did in Genesis, and Hebrews 12:24 says that Jesus' sprinkled blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. The name Jezebel also carries into the New Testament: in Revelation 2:20 the risen Christ uses it for a false prophetess in the church at Thyatira who leads his servants into immorality and idolatry. These are contrasts and echoes rather than predictions.

hard.q: The Tel Dan Stele seems to credit an Aramean king with killing Joram and Ahaziah. Does this contradict 2 Kings 9?
hard.a: The Tel Dan Stele, an Aramaic inscription found in fragments at Tel Dan in northern Israel in 1993 and 1994, contains a boast by a king of Aram, most likely Hazael, that he killed a king of Israel and a king of the house of David. Most scholars restore the damaged names as Joram son of Ahab and Ahaziah son of Jehoram. This seems to conflict with 2 Kings 9, where Jehu kills both. Several explanations have been offered. One is that Jehu acted in some kind of alliance with Hazael, or at least in the context of Hazael's war, so that Hazael could claim the deaths as his own victory; Joram's wounds, after all, came from the Arameans (8:28-29). Another is that ancient royal inscriptions routinely claimed credit for events their kings did not personally perform, and Hazael's boast is propaganda. A third is that the biblical and Aramaic accounts preserve different traditions and cannot be fully harmonized. The stele is also significant for another reason: it contains the earliest known reference outside the Bible to the house of David. Whatever the details, both sources agree that Joram and Ahaziah died violently in the same upheaval around 841 BC.

questions: Jehu said there could be no peace while idolatry and sorcery abounded. What false peace do people try to keep today while ignoring what is wrong at the root?
The judgment on Ahab's house fell years after Elijah announced it, on the very land Ahab had stolen. What does this suggest about God's patience and his justice?
Jehu was anointed by God's command and yet is portrayed with a ruthless streak. How can a person carry out God's purposes while still being accountable for how they do it?
